newsitem.title: USA: Bolivia-Brazil pipeline team urges Brazil action.
newsitem.headline: Bolivia-Brazil pipeline team urges Brazil action.

text.p: Foreign partners in the huge $5 billion Bolivia-Brazil gas pipeline project said Brazil must stop delays in opening its oil sector or risk losing financing and distribution opportunities.
Speaking at a Miami conference on the Latin American upstream Tuesday, James Barney Phillips, managing director BTB Group (Brazil), said the project's timetables were tight.
"Thirty months from now gas is to start flowing," Phillips said, noting "regulatory controls must be adequate...we need to speed these up."
"There is not a lot of time to meet mid-1997 financing (deadlines). We will urge the government to move forward."
Regulations to open the Brazilian oil sector to foreign investment are currently under government review, before being sent to the National Congress.
Optimistic estimates peg congressional approval before year's end, but Phillips said there was talk approval may not come until March next year.

BTB is a unique consortium comprised of Australia's BHP, U.S.- based Tenneco Inc and British Gas Plc, who have partnered with Brazil's state oil monopoly Petrobras and Bolivian concerns on the pipeline project.
Phillips said enormous progress on getting the pipeline constructed had occurred to date.

Brazil's financing requests are under World Bank review, tax deals have been worked out between Brazil and Bolivia, distribution contracts are signed, and pipe orders were issued in September, among others.

But the timetable points to having financing completed by mid-1997, construction start shortly after that, and completion of the Santa Cruz, Bolivia to Sao Paulo, Brazil section finished by the end of 1998.
"All of us have to understand this is like a puzzle, fitting commercial and political prospects into the project," said Phillips.

Of the total project's estimated cost, only $2 billion is for the actual pipeline, with $1 billion seen for developing gas reserves in Bolivia, another $2 billion for power plant conversion, and a final $700 million for creating an industrial distribution system.
BTB and Petrobras hope to shift the electricity sector in Brazil away from the now dominant hydroelectric source, and ultimately to create markets for gas currently non-existent.
Brazil uses 12 million cubic meters of gas per day, a miniscule amount of the nation's energy usage rate.
The government has set a goal to up that amount to 85 million cubic meters per day by the year 2005.
Petrobras holds 51 pct of the Brazilian share of the venture, with BTB at 25 pct, Enron and YPFB at 20 pct and other Brazilian companies at 4 pct.
For the Bolivian part of the venture, YPFB holds 85 pct, and BTB/Petrobras a 15 pct total.
